content: The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes the importance of standardized clinical data collection to enhance the understanding of disease characteristics, progression, and the effects of treatments, including adverse events. This approach is particularly relevant in the clinical management of diphtheria, as outlined in the WHO guidelines. The WHO Steering Committee, comprising representatives from regional offices and headquarters, provided technical expertise. Key members include Janet Diaz (Clinical Management Team Lead, Health Emergencies Programme), Silvia Bertagnolio (Clinical Team for COVID-19 Response), and other experts from fields such as antimicrobial resistance, immunization, public health laboratory strengthening, and health logistics. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included global experts such as Umma Idris Abdullahi (Federal Medical Centre, Nigeria), Hamed Hassan Adetola (Ministry of Health, Sierra Leone), Andrew Argent (University of Cape Town, South Africa), and others from institutions worldwide. These experts contributed their knowledge in infectious diseases, public health, and clinical management. The project officer, Julie Viry, oversaw the Clinical Management Team at WHO headquarters. The Steering Committee was responsible for decisions regarding guideline production and convening the GDG. Methodological guidance was provided by Gordon Guyatt (McMaster University, Canada), while Srinivas Murthy (University of British Columbia, Canada) served as the Clinical Chair. Andrew Owen (Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, UK) acted as the Technical Advisor. Systematic reviewers, including Lindsay Keegan (University of Utah, USA) and Shaun Truelove (Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, USA), conducted evidence reviews. External reviewers, such as Richard Kojan (Alliance for International Medical Action, Democratic Republic of the Congo) and Sushil Kabra (New Delhi, India), provided additional insights. The guideline development was supported by funding from the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE). The references cited in the guideline include key studies and resources on diphtheria, such as vaccine-preventable disease surveillance standards, laboratory manuals for diagnosis, and systematic reviews on clinical and epidemiological aspects of diphtheria. These references also include studies on antimicrobial resistance, treatment comparisons (e.g., penicillin vs. erythromycin), and outbreak responses in various regions. The guideline reflects a comprehensive effort to address the clinical management of diphtheria, incorporating global expertise, evidence-based practices, and lessons learned from past outbreaks.
